definition: A computer-assisted proof is a mathematical proof that has been at least partially generated by computer.
details: Most computer-aided proofs to date have been implementations of large proofs-by-exhaustion of a mathematical theorem. The idea is to use a computer program to perform lengthy computations, and to provide a proof that the result of these computations implies the given theorem. In 1976, the four color theorem was the first major theorem to be verified using a computer program. Attempts have also been made in the area of artificial intelligence research to create smaller, explicit, new proofs of mathematical theorems from the bottom up using automated reasoning techniques such as heuristic search. Such automated theorem provers have proved a number of new results and found new proofs for known theorems. Additionally, interactive proof assistants allow mathematicians to develop human-readable proofs which are nonetheless formally verified for correctness. Since these proofs are generally human-surveyable (albeit with difficulty, as with the proof of the Robbins conjecture) they do not share the controversial implications of computer-aided proofs-by-exhaustion.

explainer.lead: A computer-assisted proof uses a computer to generate at least part of a mathematical proof. This makes it possible to handle extremely long calculations, search for new proofs, or formally check proofs written by people.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a puzzle with far too many cases for anyone to check by hand. A computer can work through those cases, while the proof explains why its answers settle the puzzle. Computers can also help discover proofs or check that each step in a human-written proof is correct.
tiers.practitioner: Automated theorem provers use techniques such as heuristic search to discover new results or alternative proofs, while interactive proof assistants support human-readable proofs with formal correctness checks. Proofs by exhaustion can involve computations that are difficult for people to survey, and even formally verified proofs can be hard to follow, as with the proof of the Robbins conjecture.
tiers.paperLevel: A proof P is computer-assisted if at least part of P is generated by computer. For proof by exhaustion, a program performs a lengthy computation C, and the proof establishes that the result of C implies the target theorem; the 1976 verification of the four color theorem was the first major theorem verified this way. Large exhaustive proofs can be controversial because they are difficult to survey, whereas interactive proof assistants generally produce human-surveyable, formally verified proofs, though sometimes with difficulty.

explainer.example: The four color theorem was verified using a computer program in 1976. The program performed the lengthy case-checking computation, and the accompanying proof established that its result implied the theorem.

explainer.intuition: Some proofs require more calculation than a person can reasonably complete, while others benefit from a machine searching for steps or checking them. The mathematical argument must still connect the computer's work to the theorem.
howItWorks: State the theorem to be proved.
Choose exhaustive computation, automated proof search, or interactive proof development.
Use a program to calculate, search, or formally check the proof.
Show why the resulting work establishes the theorem.
explainer.whyItMatters: Computer assistance extends proof beyond practical human calculation limits and has produced both new mathematical results and new proofs of known theorems. It also raises questions about how easily a proof can be inspected and understood by people.
misconceptions: It does not always mean exhaustive case-checking; computers can also discover or formally verify proofs.
A formally verified proof is not necessarily easy for a person to read or survey.
